<reason>Side B won decisively by exposing the flawed incentive structure of the proposition. Because the motion regulates a voluntary marketing claim rather than mandating operational cuts (which Side A conceded in [A4.1]), Side B proved that imposing impossible in-value-chain requirements on hard-to-abate sectors like aviation and cement would simply cause firms to abandon their net-zero pledges. Side A walked into several major traps: arguing that profit-driven boards would continue funding billions in external removals as uncredited "philanthropy" [A3.1, A4.1], insisting on capping even 100% verified and permanent physical carbon removal [A2.5, A4.2], and claiming that companies merely dropping the net-zero title "cools the planet" [A5.3]. Side B ruthlessly capitalized on each of these points, demonstrating that regulating offset quality rather than quantity harnesses private capital for real atmospheric removals, whereas a volume cap leaves operational emissions unchanged while evaporating vital climate finance.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>In [B4.4]-[B4.5], Side B dismantled Side A's argument in [A4.2] that even verified, permanent ton-for-ton removal must be capped lest a company expand from emitting one ton to two tons. Side B showed that if an expanding firm emits two tons and permanently removes two tons, net atmospheric impact remains zero while removal funding doubles—whereas under Side A's celebrated alternative where the firm "exits the claim," the firm still expands to emit those same two tons of carbon while removing zero.</best_rebuttal>
